correctness.rationale: The Lipschitz norm is the maximum cross-edge difference. Tight edges characterize vertices, yielding exactly one constant class and the other at signs ±1 (or two constant classes differing by one). Every vertex has \(Q_0=1\). Cross-edge coordinate dual norm relative to \(Q_0\) is \(\sqrt d\), so the two-sided comparison holds; a displayed vector attains the lower extreme. Symmetrizing any competitor over \(S_m\times S_n\) does not increase its distortion. Positive invariant forms have three positive coefficients, and balanced-sign vertices force inequalities bounding them. The resulting edge functional dual norm is at least \(d\) for every competitor, which supplies the global lower bound. The proof covers all \(m,n\ge3\); 6,228 exact-rational consistency checks were replayed from the included source, but are not a substitute for the proof.

originality.rationale: The conclusion gives the exact Euclidean Hilbert-distance formula for all unit-edge \(K_{m,n}\) with both part sizes at least three. The graph-polytope and Hanner classification of arXiv:1911.10642 supplies structural context but contains neither the invariant ellipsoid formula nor the sharp Hilbert comparison; \(K_{m,n}\) in this regime is not a spiderweb or a tree-like gluing of spiderwebs. The Banach–Mazur comparisons in arXiv:1807.03814 are to \(\ell_1\) rather than \(\ell_2\); arXiv:0904.3178 concerns trees. Published records about bipartite numerical index or cycle numerical index do not imply a precise Hilbert distance. An earlier real cycle Hilbert-distance classification deals with different canonical graph edge/cycle structures. The result is not guaranteed globally unpublished, and an older equivalent convex-body statement remains a risk.
residual_risks: An unindexed pre-2009/2016 convex-body theorem for bipartite graph-root polytopes or a general equality condition in John’s Euclidean-distance theorem might offer equivalent coverage.

value.rationale: Real graph transportation spaces furnish an intrinsic Banach–Mazur invariant; the complete bipartite family includes non-Hanner, multi-cycle configurations in every dimension \(d=m+n-1\ge5\). The exact distance reaches the universal John threshold \(\sqrt d\) despite absence of the known Hanner/spiderweb decompositions, and its invariant ellipsoid and sharp dual norm are fully explicit. This answers a natural exact extremal-geometry question for a two-parameter graph class rather than an unmotivated finite slice. It does not claim a new invariant for already-understood trees or spiderwebs, nor a universal bipartite statement.
